nodes.label: Probability, Distributions and Statistics
nodes.note: Axiomatic probability, conditional probability, Bayes, random variables, binomial and related distributions, and descriptive statistics. Each PYQ leans on one definition and one theorem.

nodes.label: Probability Foundations
nodes.note: Sample space, events, and the axioms.

nodes.label: Sample Space and Events
nodes.note: The sample space S is all outcomes; an event E is a subset: $$P(E) = \frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$$ for equally likely outcomes. Sure event $P(S)=1$, impossible event $P(\emptyset)=0$.

nodes.label: Mutually Exclusive and Exhaustive Events
nodes.note: Disjoint events never co-occur: $$A \cap B = \emptyset \Rightarrow P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$$. Exhaustive events cover S, so their probabilities sum to 1.

nodes.label: Addition Theorem for Events
nodes.note: $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$. Extends to three events with the full inclusion-exclusion pattern.

nodes.label: Classical vs Empirical Probability
nodes.note: Classical probability assumes equally likely outcomes, while empirical probability uses observed frequency: $$P(E) \approx \frac{\text{favourable trials}}{\text{total trials}}$$. Law of large numbers justifies the approximation.

nodes.label: Odds in Favour and Against
nodes.note: Odds convert probabilities: $$\text{odds in favour} = \frac{P(E)}{1 - P(E)}$$. A probability $3/7$ corresponds to odds $3 : 4$ in favour.

nodes.label: Complement Rule
nodes.note: $$P(\bar{A}) = 1 - P(A)$$ resolves 'at least one' counts: compute the none-case and subtract.

nodes.label: Conditional Probability and Bayes
nodes.note: Dependence, independence, and updating.

nodes.label: Conditional Probability
nodes.note: $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \ P(B) > 0$$. It reweights the space to outcomes where B already happened.

nodes.label: Tree Diagrams
nodes.note: Sequential experiments draw branching trees; probabilities along a branch multiply, and probabilities of distinct branches add. Two-stage draws of balls from an urn are standard tree-diagram items.

nodes.label: Multiplication Rule
nodes.note: Chain of conditional probabilities: $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$$. Drawing balls without replacement uses it directly.

nodes.label: Independence of Events
nodes.note: A and B are independent when $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$$. Independent coin tosses and dice rolls are the canonical examples.

nodes.label: Law of Total Probability
nodes.note: For a partition $\{E_i\}$ of S: $$P(A) = \sum_i P(E_i)\,P(A \mid E_i)$$. Bayes problems always start with this expansion in the denominator.

nodes.label: Example: Two Machines
nodes.note: Machine A makes 60% of parts with 2% defect, B makes 40% with 5% defect. $P(A \mid \text{defect}) = \frac{0.6 \cdot 0.02}{0.6 \cdot 0.02 + 0.4 \cdot 0.05} = \frac{3}{8}$.

nodes.label: Bayes' Theorem
nodes.note: $$P(E_i \mid A) = \frac{P(E_i)P(A \mid E_i)}{\sum_j P(E_j)P(A \mid E_j)}$$. Use it to invert cause and effect, e.g. defect rates across two machines.

nodes.label: Random Variables and Expectation
nodes.note: From experiments to numeric outcomes.

nodes.label: Discrete Random Variable
nodes.note: A variable X mapping outcomes to numbers has a probability mass function $p(x) = P(X = x)$ with $\sum p(x) = 1$. Number of heads in 3 tosses is the standard RV.

nodes.label: Expectation (Mean)
nodes.note: $$E(X) = \sum_i x_i\, p(x_i)$$ is the long-run average. Linearity $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$ simplifies most JEE items.

nodes.label: Variance and Standard Deviation
nodes.note: $$\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = \sum (x_i - \mu)^2 p(x_i)$$. SD is the square root of variance, so variance questions often test the shortcut formula.

nodes.label: Example: Expected Winnings
nodes.note: A game pays Rs 100 with probability 0.1 and loses Rs 20 with 0.9: $E = 0.1(100) - 0.9(20) = -8$, so it is unfavourable on average.

nodes.label: Distribution Tables
nodes.note: A valid distribution lists all x_i with probabilities summing to 1. Unknown constants in such problems come from $\sum p(x_i) = 1$.

nodes.label: Binomial Distribution
nodes.note: Bernoulli trials counted over n repetitions.

nodes.label: Bernoulli and Binomial Trials
nodes.note: Each trial has success probability p and failure q = 1 - p, independent of others. n trials give the binomial setting.

nodes.label: Binomial Probability Mass Function
nodes.note: $$P(X = r) = {}^nC_r\, p^r q^{\,n-r}$$. The probability of exactly r successes in n trials drives every JEE binomial PYQ.

nodes.label: Mean and Variance of Binomial
nodes.note: $$E(X) = np, \quad \text{Var}(X) = npq$$. Maximum probability occurs at the integer part of $(n+1)p$.

nodes.label: At Least One Success
nodes.note: $$P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - q^n$$. Use the complement instead of summing the binomial tail.

nodes.label: Example: Coin Tosses
nodes.note: Probability of exactly 3 heads in 5 tosses: ${}^5C_3 (1/2)^3 (1/2)^2 = \frac{10}{32} = \frac{5}{16}$.

nodes.label: Other Distributions
nodes.note: Poisson, geometric, and normal appear as named limits or models.

nodes.label: Poisson Distribution
nodes.note: $$P(X = r) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^r}{r!}$$ models rare events with rate lambda. It arises as the $n \to \infty, p \to 0$ limit of binomial.

nodes.label: Normal Distribution
nodes.note: A continuous curve with mean mu and SD sigma; about 68% of data lies within one sigma. Standardizing with $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ converts lookups to the standard normal table.

nodes.label: Example: Standardisation
nodes.note: If marks are $N(60, 10^2)$, then $P(X \ge 80) = P(Z \ge 2) \approx 0.0228$ from the standard normal table.

nodes.label: Geometric Distribution
nodes.note: Number of trials until the first success: $$P(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1} p$$. Its mean $1/p$ measures waiting time for the first success.

nodes.label: Statistics
nodes.note: Central tendency, dispersion, and correlation.

nodes.label: Mean, Median and Mode
nodes.note: Mean $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i$, median is the middle ordered value, mode the most frequent. Skewed JEE data questions often distinguish which one misleads.

nodes.label: Variance, SD and Range
nodes.note: $$\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2$$ and the computational form $\sigma^2 = \overline{x^2} - \bar{x}^2$. Coefficient of variation $CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$ compares data sets.

nodes.label: Correlation
nodes.note: $$r = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}}$$ lies in $[-1, 1]$: $r = 1$ perfect positive linear relation, $r = -1$ perfect negative, $r = 0$ no linear relation.

nodes.label: Weighted Mean
nodes.note: Combine group means with weights: $$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i}$$. JEE uses it for combined averages of two sections with different sizes.

nodes.label: Coefficient of Variation
nodes.note: $$CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$$ compares relative spread of two data sets. The set with higher CV is less consistent.

nodes.label: Regression Lines
nodes.note: Least-squares lines of y on x and x on y both pass through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$: $$y - \bar{y} = r\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}(x - \bar{x})$$. The product of the two slopes is $r^2$.
